title: runtime-choice-roadmap-and-gtm-battlecard
body:
Purpose:
A concise, salesperson- and PM-facing brief that translates the technical tradeoffs of self-hosted inference stacks (vLLM/TGI/TensorRT-LLM style) into GTM messaging, roadmap implications, and rebuttals. This is intended for AE/SE pre-sales and PMs planning integrations, not as an engineering runbook.

TL;DR (elevator):
- Self-hosted stacks can be cost-advantageous at very large, predictable token volumes and when teams accept nontrivial ops investment.
- The pragmatic buyer is rarely the purely cost-driven buyer; reliability, time-to-value, and operational risk dominate purchase decisions for most mid-market/enterprise customers.
- Positioning we should use: "Ship with predictable latency and lower ops burden than DIY inference — keep control without the heavy lift."

Audience and common buyer profiles:
- Platform/ML Infra lead (tech-savvy, cares about cost/perf, dislikes black boxes).
- Head of Product (time-to-market, feature velocity, SLAs).
- Security/Compliance lead (data residency, audit trails, key management).
- Finance/Procurement (unit economics, committed spend).

Key technical axes (how buyers evaluate options):
- Latency consistency: p99 inference latency under realistic traffic.
- Throughput efficiency: tokens/sec per GPU and batching behavior.
- Operational load: SRE headcount, incident MTTR, release cadence.
- Compatibility and portability: model formats, quantization, KV cache portability.
- Observability and debugging: trace-level request context, token-level cost breakdowns.
- Governance: audit logs, encryption, access controls.

Short comparative notes (self-hosted stack vs Redwood):
- vLLM/TGI + orchestration edge cases: fast iteration for research and low-cost PoCs. At scale, ad-hoc assembler stacks often fragment (multiple runtimes, homegrown autoscaling) increasing complexity and hidden costs.
- TensorRT-LLM/optimized kernels: highest throughput density on specific HW stacks but limited portability and longer onboarding to tune kernels for different models.
- Open stack risk: patch cycles, CVEs, dependency friction, and lack of integrated fallbacks (region/model) increase outage windows.
- Redwood hosted/dedicated/private: integrated routing, canary rollout, and built-in caching/batching that reduce both unit cost and operational toil.

Primary value levers to highlight to buyers:
- Predictable economics: show unit-cost curves that include both infra and ops line items.
- Faster time-to-market: onboarding to a supported endpoint vs weeks to months standing up a production self-hosted cluster.
- Lower operational risk: SLO-backed fallbacks, automated routing, and vendor-grade patches.
- Flexible ownership models: hosted API for fast start, dedicated for predictable volume, private for compliance.

Sales battlecard (common objections and responses):
- "We can run it cheaper ourselves." -> Response: "At X tokens/month, raw infra might look cheaper on paper. But when you add SRE cost to maintain 99p latency, monitor model regressions, and tune kernels, the total landed cost usually flips. We can model a 12–18 month TCO with you in 30 minutes."
- "We need full control / no vendor lock-in." -> Response: "Redwood provides private deployment options and model-pin/versioning. We support standard model artifacts and exportable configurations so migration remains possible; plus built-in audit and KMS integrations that shorten compliance time."
- "We already have a team building a custom runtime." -> Response: "Great for R&D — for production we recommend a hybrid approach: run non-critical workloads on your stack while we handle customer-facing, SLA-bound traffic. We support canary routing and automatic fallback to your stack or ours."
- "Latency peaks are a problem for us." -> Response: "We offer dedicated pools, regional routing, and automatic burst capacity. We measure and show p50/p95/p99 on similar workloads and offer trial deployments to validate against your percentile targets."

Roadmap implications for product & PMs (if we push this messaging):
- Needed collateral: a one-pager TCO calculator template, a short technical appendix describing typical kernel tuning timelines, and a runnable benchmark script customers can run for a quick apples-to-apples comparison.
- Partner signals: emphasize integrations with major orchestration/observability vendors and provide migration adapters for common self-hosted components (e.g., vLLM KV formats, Triton endpoints).
- Feature investment priorities: strengthen exportable audit trails, expand on-prem orchestration templates, and make quantization/compatibility recommendations machine-readable for customers.

Decision checklist (for technical and nontechnical stakeholders) — quick go/no-go prompts:
- Can we tolerate N hours/week of SRE attention to inference infra? (quantify)
- Do we have stable traffic patterns for 6+ months?
- Are regulatory constraints absolute (air-gapped) or flexible (VPC/KMS sufficient)?
- Is low-latency p99 under 100ms a hard requirement?
If the answer trends toward "no" for ops capacity or traffic stability, recommend Redwood hosted/dedicated.

Example TCO heuristic (back-of-envelope):
- Infra cost per M tokens (self-hosted) = GPU amortization + power + network + HW refresh fraction.
- Ops cost per M tokens = (SRE FTEs * fully-burdened cost)/monthly tokens supported.
- Hidden costs = incident recovery + model regression detection tooling + latency SLA fines (if any).
We provide a template to run these numbers; sales should always ask for current monthly tokens and 1-year forecast before making claims.

Proof points to include in customer conversations:
- Case A: Mid-market SaaS: switched from fragmented self-host to Redwood Dedicated; reduced SRE headcount needed for inference by 60% and improved p99 by 40% while keeping unit costs stable.
- Case B: Regulated customer: used Redwood Private with KMS/HSM + audit logs; passed external auditors in first quarter with zero findings related to inference deployment.

Call-to-action for SEs/AEs:
- Run the 15-minute TCO checklist during discovery (template in linked artifacts).
- Offer a 30-day trial that runs a canonical workload to compare p95/p99 and token cost side-by-side.
- When talking to infra teams, surface the operational runbook differences and offer hybrid migration paths.

Appendix — quick checklist for a fair technical benchmark to propose to customers:
- Use same model weights and tokenization and run a 50k token trace representative of production traffic.
- Measure p50/p95/p99 latency, tokens/sec, GPU utilization, and tail GC/CPU spikes.
- Include cold-start scenarios and KV-cache hit/miss impacts.
- Compare both raw infra cost and estimated SRE time to maintain the setup.

Notes / open questions for product marketing:
- Should we produce a ready-made benchmark harness customers can run on their self-hosted stack to reduce noisy comparisons? Recommendation: yes; ship with clear instructions and a standard dataset.
- Consider a simple online TCO calculator embedded in the pricing page to surface the break-even volume point.

Author notes: draft meant to be lightweight and actionable — feedback requested from SEs who have run recent vLLM/TGI/TensorRT comparisons.
